# Atelectasis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Pulmonology > Other pulmonologic disorders > Atelectasis*

[Original Article Link](/library/sM0tJg)

---

## Summary

Atelectasis is a loss of <u>lung</u> volume that may be caused by a variety of ventilation disorders, for instance, bronchial injury or an obstructive mass such as a <u>tumor</u>. It may be categorized as obstructive, nonobstructive, postoperative, or rounded. Clinical features depend on the severity and extent of atelectasis, ranging from no symptoms to <u>respiratory distress</u>. <u>Physical examination</u> reveals a <u>dull note on percussion</u> and diminished breathing sounds over the affected area. On <u>x-ray</u>, the atelectatic section of the <u>lung</u> appears condensed and, due to decreased <u>lung</u> volume, may extend to the surrounding tissue. This effect can lead to an elevated <u>diaphragm</u> and <u>mediastinal</u> shift to the affected side. Treatment depends on the underlying cause. Complications of atelectasis include <u>pneumonia</u> or, depending on the extent of disease, <u>respiratory failure</u>.

---

## Etiology

* Obstructive atelectasis (most common): <u>airway obstruction</u> (e.g., by a foreign body, mucus plug, <u>malignancy</u>) → nonventilated <u>alveoli</u> → reabsorption of gas in the poststenotic space → <u>lung</u> collapse

* Nonobstructive atelectasis

* <u>Compression atelectasis</u>: external space-occupying lesion (e.g., <u>pleural effusion</u>) that compresses the <u>lung</u> → forcefully pushes air out of the <u>alveoli</u>

* <u>Adhesive atelectasis</u>: <u>surfactant deficiency</u> or dysfunction → increases surface tension of <u>alveoli</u> → instability and collapse (e.g., <u>acute respiratory distress syndrome</u> (<u>ARDS</u>) in adults, <u>respiratory distress</u> syndrome in <u>premature infants</u>)

* Cicatrization (contraction) atelectasis: <u>parenchymal</u> scarring that leads to contraction of the <u>lung</u> (due to chronic destructive <u>lung</u> processes such as <u>tuberculosis</u>, <u>sarcoidosis</u>, and <u>fibrosis</u>, e.g., secondary to <u>radiation therapy</u>)

* <u>Relaxation atelectasis</u>: loss of contact between parietal and <u>visceral</u> tissue (e.g., <u>pneumothorax</u>, <u>pleural effusion</u>)

* <u>Replacement atelectasis</u>: All the <u>alveoli</u> in an entire lobe are replaced by <u>tumor</u> (e.g., bronchioloalveolar cell <u>carcinoma</u>) → loss of volume → <u>lung</u> collapse

* Postoperative atelectasis: one of the most common post-operative complications (especially after chest or abdominal <u>surgery</u>); often occurs within 72 hours of <u>surgery</u>

* Rounded atelectasis: folding of the atelectatic <u>lung tissue</u> (with fibrous bands and adhesions) to the <u>pleura</u> (e.g., <u>asbestosis</u>)

* Middle lobe syndrome: intraluminal or extraluminal obstruction or no identifiable cause of obstruction → recurrent or fixed atelectasis of the right middle lobe and/or lingula (e.g., associated with childhood <u>asthma</u>, Sjögren syndrome)

## Clinical features

* Symptoms depend on the acuity and extent of atelectasis.

* Small number of affected <u>alveoli</u> or slowly manifesting atelectasis → asymptomatic or minimal symptoms

* Large number of affected <u>alveoli</u> or rapid onset → acute <u>dyspnea</u>, <u>chest pain</u>, <u>tachypnea</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, and <u>cyanosis</u>

* <u>Dull percussion note</u>, diminished breath sounds, and decreased <u>fremitus</u> over the affected <u>lung</u>

* Possibly <u>tracheal deviation</u> towards the side of lesion

---

## Diagnosis

* <u>Arterial blood gas analysis</u>

* <u>Hypoxemia</u>, potentially low <u>PaCO<sub>2</sub></u>, and <u>respiratory alkalosis</u>

* <u>Alveoli</u> that are unable to participate in <u>gas exchange</u> → decreased <u>V/Q ratio</u> (<u>V/Q mismatch</u>) → <u>hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction</u> → shunting of blood away from poorly ventilated <u>alveoli</u>

* Imaging findings in atelectasis (e.g., <u>chest x-ray</u>, CT chest): evidence of lobar collapse ;  [[3]](/library/3m0S2g)

* Direct signs: displacement of fissures and homogeneous opacification of the collapsed lobe

* Indirect signs

* Elevation of <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>diaphragm</u>

* Displacement of the hilum and <u>mediastinal</u> structures towards the affected side

* Loss of volume in the affected side of the chest

* Increased lucency and overinflation of the unaffected <u>lung</u>; silhouetting of the <u>diaphragm</u> or the <u>heart</u> border

* <u>Bronchoscopy</u> (diagnostic and therapeutic): A <u>biopsy</u> may be performed if the etiology is uncertain despite imaging (e.g., to exclude <u>malignancy</u>) and mucus plugs can be removed. [[4]](/library/im0J2g)

## Treatment

* Adequate <u>analgesia</u>

* Early mobilization

* <u>Lung</u> expansion maneuvers that increase positive end-expiratory pressure (<u>PEEP</u>) 

* Deep breathing exercises

* Directed <u>coughing</u>

* Intermittent <u>incentive spirometry</u>

* <u>Continuous positive airway pressure</u> (<u>CPAP</u>) for patients unable to perform deep breathing exercises.

* Treatment of underlying condition

* See <u>foreign body aspiration</u>, <u>pleural effusion</u>, <u>pneumothorax</u>, etc.

* <u>Bronchoscopy</u> to remove tumors causing obstructive or <u>compression atelectasis</u>





> [!NOTE]
> The risk of atelectasis after <u>surgery</u> can be avoided by prescribing <u>opioids</u> in doses that are sufficient for <u>pain</u> relief, as well as encouraging the use of <u>incentive spirometry</u>. At the same time, <u>opioids</u> should be used with caution due to their suppression on <u>coughing</u>. Smoking should be avoided 6–8 weeks prior to <u>surgery</u>.

---

## Complications

* <u>Pneumonia</u>

* <u>Lung abscess</u>

* <u>Respiratory failure</u>




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Prevention of post-operative atelectasis

* Preoperative

* <u>Smoking cessation</u> prior to elective <u>surgery</u> (6–8 weeks)

* <u>Physical therapy</u> (e.g, breathing and aerobic exercises)

* Treatment of poorly controlled <u>asthma</u>, symptomatic <u>COPD</u>, and respiratory chest infections.

* See also “<u>Preoperative management</u>.”

* Intraoperative: ventilation with <u>PEEP</u>

* Postoperative [[7]](/library/Tt161i0)

* <u>Incentive spirometry</u> (most important)

* <u>Pain control</u>

* Adequate mobilization

* See also “<u>Postoperative preventive measures</u>.”
